title: Learning singers from a neighbour's records in Fitzgerald
summary: He heard Ethel Waters, Caruso, Ellington and others on a neighbour's graphinola in return for running errands, which got him jazz oriented.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Where had you heare these performers?

Well, in Fitzgerald, Georgia, a lady used to play a record. She had a graphinola, and she used to let me play records, you know. I used to run errands for her. She liked White Castle hamburgers, was a nice old lady, she was, and she says that her husband was in import -- export and import, whatever. And he had all these kind of records, and she would let me -- that was kind of like a tip, you know.

But she loved them -- those White Castle hamburgers. At that time I think they was about seven cents a piece, two for 12 cents, something like that, they had. And she was letting me play these records, you see. And I got familiar with these different people, singers, the famous ones, you know, and I heard all of them at that time -- Ethel Waters, as I said, and Morton Downey, and I even heard the famous Irish singer -- what's his name -- and Caruso, Enrico Caruso at the time, you know.

But I mean, you know, I couldn't sing like him, you see, because he was -- I heard Duke Ellington -- he was with the McKinney's Cotton Pickers at the time. So I think I got jazz oriented from listening at those records, you see, recordings. And --
Yeah, I was very young, but I was large for my size, because, see, my mother kind of set a record
